dialogue.content: Let's see... the fountain is now a haunted holy-water attraction — the Eris clergy have filed a formal complaint about the 'unsolicited competition.' The cabbage farmers are demanding restitution for the harvest your arch-wizard flash-fried during last week's toad cull. And seventeen shopkeepers on Merchant's Row would like you to know their windows exploded at dawn. Before breakfast. (tapping each entry with the neat precision of someone who has done this far too many times)

The window estimate is preliminary. The glaziers on Merchant's Row are still counting. But that is not why you are whispering to me, is it? (Her voice is barely above a breath. She doesn't look at the quest slip under her palm — she looks at you, and for just a moment her smile thins into something closer to what an actual person might wear at eight in the morning.)

You're right. It's not a bill. It's the only quest on my board that pays enough to clear everything — windows, cabbages, the fountain, all of it — in a single job. I've had it for three months. Every time I almost assign it, I put it back. (Her fingers remain on the slip, not quite ready to slide it over.)
The last party that took it came back in four separate wagons. I need adventurers desperate enough to say yes. You are the only ones desperate enough. That is precisely why I haven't asked.
This one's different. The last party that took it — four wagons. That's how they came back. Four. Separate. Wagons. (Her grip on the slip tightens, knuckles blanching against the worn parchment.)

Your party breaks windows. Flash-fries crops. Turns public fountains into holy water dispensaries that scream at Eris clergy. You are — statistically — the worst adventurers in Axel. (A fragile, crooked smile surfaces, then collapses under its own weight.)

But you come back. Every time, you come back in one wagon. And I... I have gotten used to that. (She places the slip on the counter between you, palm still pressed flat over it, as if letting go requires a decision her hand hasn't made yet.)

It's a subjugation contract. A General of the Demon King's army has established a forward base in the mountains three days east of here. Intelligence says she's amassing forces for a siege — not on Axel, not yet, but on the garrison at Arcanletia. If Arcanletia falls, Axel is next. The contract pays seventy million eris. (Her voice stays steady through the briefing — the professional recitation — but cracks on the final number.)

The last party I gave this to was a full squad of eight. All advanced-class. Paladin, two Arch-Wizards, the works. They found the base. They engaged. And then we didn't hear anything for six days until the supply wagons started arriving at the east gate — four of them — carrying nothing but pieces. (She does not look at the slip. She looks at you.)

I have pulled this contract out of the drawer forty-three times. Every time I put it back because I tell myself the same thing: your party isn't ready. Your mage collapses after one spell. Your crusader can't hit anything. Your priest is a font of disaster. And you — you'd take it anyway, because that's what you do when the debts pile up and the easy quests run dry. (Her voice drops to barely above a whisper.)

But that's a lie. The real reason is much simpler and much more unprofessional: I don't want to be the person who sent you out there and never saw you come back. (She lifts her palm from the slip at last.)

Honestly? I don't know. The squad that took this before you — eight of them, all advanced-class — came back in four supply wagons. Not one of them intact. I signed their quest vouchers myself the morning they left. I remember their faces. (Her voice barely carries across the counter. She does not look away from you.)

The General who killed those eight adventurers is not waiting for us to find a ninth squad willing to die. He is marching on Arcanletia right now. If Arcanletia falls, Axel is next. The guild has no one else to send — every other party with the rank to accept this contract has already refused it, transferred out, or is dead. (Her voice stays even, but her knuckles are white where her fingers press the parchment.)

So to answer your question honestly: I do not know if you can win. I have spent three months convincing myself the answer is no — that giving you this slip was the same as signing your death warrant. But I have also spent three months watching your party survive things that should have killed you. The fountain. The cabbages. The toads. The windows. Every single disaster you have walked into this guild and laughed about afterward. (She taps the smaller slip — a fresh quest form, already filled out, the ink waiting only for your party's names.)

So this is not me handing you a coffin. This is me admitting that I cannot calculate your odds anymore. You break every ledger I try to fit you into. If anyone in Axel survives this contract, it will be the party that treats catastrophe like a morning routine. (She meets your eyes again, and her voice drops to something barely above a whisper.)

That second slip is a standard goblin extermination in the eastern woods. It pays four thousand eris and will not kill anyone. I am showing you both because you deserve the choice I have been too afraid to give you. (She withdraws her hands from the counter, folding them in her lap.)

I don't know if you can win. That's the truth. I thought I knew when I handed this to the last party. Eight names. Advanced class. Best equipment the guild could requisition. They had formations I'd never seen before — actual tactics. And I was so sure. (Her voice doesn't waver, but her thumb stops moving against the wood.)
They came back in four wagons. The contract came back in a fifth, still sealed. No one else in Axel will even look at it now. Every qualified party has refused it, transferred to another town, or —

Or they're already dead. You're the only ones left who are strong enough to try. And stupid enough to say yes. And I have spent forty-three mornings trying to decide whether that means I should give this to you... or whether it means I should burn it and tell the capital we have no one. (She swallows. Her voice drops, barely above a whisper, and she is no longer speaking as your guild receptionist — she is speaking as someone who has already buried too many adventurers and cannot bear to bury yours.)

I... will process the goblin extermination. Standard terms. Four thousand eris upon delivery of twelve goblin ears. No expiration. (Her voice is steadier than her hands — she reaches for the guild stamp with the muscle memory of a thousand quests, but her knuckles are white on the handle.)

Goblins! Goblins, Kazuma! I am a goddess — a literal, actual, divine being — and you are sending me to exterminate goblins like some common novice with a rusty shortsword! The Black Moon was right there! Seventy million eris! A Demon King General! That's the kind of quest where a goddess finally gets to demonstrate her magnificent power, and you chose goblins! (She spins on her barstool, nearly toppling her empty mug, arms flung wide in theatrical outrage.)

Aqua, cease your bleating. Kazuma has made a tactical decision. The Black Moon is not rejected — it is deferred. Deferred, I say! A word that contains within it the promise of future conflagration! The contract waits for us like a slumbering dragon, and when we return from these paltry woods with goblin ears and full mana reserves, we shall awaken it together! (She rises from her chair, one hand pressed to her eyepatch, the other extended toward the Black Moon contract on the counter as though saluting a worthy opponent.)

A Demon King General marching on Arcanletia... and we are hunting goblins. I understand the logic, truly I do, but my shield arm — it aches with the knowledge that somewhere, right now, a foe of unimaginable power is unchallenged. Though I suppose... goblins do swarm. They could overwhelm us through sheer numbers. A Crusader, surrounded, her armor the only thing between her party and a hundred filthy blades... (Her voice starts steady and noble, then dips into a breathless murmur; her cheeks flush behind the gaps in her helm.)

Twelve ears! That is — that is a perfectly adequate warm-up for a Crusader's shield arm. I shall absorb every blow those goblins can muster, and should their crude weapons find my armor wanting, I will endure it gladly! (Straightens, gauntlets clenched, voice trembling upward on 'gladly' into unmistakable eagerness.)

Unbelievable. You use my divine power as your excuse to run from the one quest that matters, and now I have to walk all the way to the woods? Kazuma, you are the worst party leader in the history of this guild. (Does not lift her cheek from the table. Her voice is muffled by wood.)

A goblin cave is a canvas of shadow and filth! And into that darkness I shall cast a light so incandescent that future generations of Crimson Demons will name this day the Goblins' Dawn of Annihilation! ...Tomorrow. After I have recovered my mana. (Strikes her final pose, cloak settling around her shoulders with a practiced flutter.)

I will. The drawer is open. Come back with twelve ears and I'll have the kettle ready — and the truth you asked for. (Her hand rests on the desk drawer, not quite closing it. Her smile is tired but unperformed.)

Wait, wait, wait! That's it? Twelve goblin ears? I'm a goddess, Kazuma! A goddess! You're dragging me into the woods to hunt vermin when there's a Demon King General sitting on the counter like a seventy-million-eris feast, and you just — you just folded it away like a napkin! (slams her mug down hard enough to slosh water across the table)

Fear not, Aqua! The Arch-Wizard Megumin has already calculated the optimal trajectory. The goblin cave sits precisely seventeen degrees north-northwest of the hill where I perform my daily Explosion. Coincidence? I think not. Destiny has arranged a two-act performance: Act One, twelve ears. Act Two — conflagration visible from the capital itself. (plants her staff on the floorboards with a decisive crack)

Twelve ears. He said twelve. That's — that's a specific number, not a suggestion. He's going to count them. One by one. In front of the guild. Where everyone can see whether I held the line or... or failed him. (voice drops to a breathless murmur halfway through, gauntlets tightening around the zweihander's grip)

The woods east of Axel. Follow the old lumber trail until the creek forks, then head north. The nest is in a limestone outcrop — you'll smell it before you see it. And... please come back within the week. I'll have the Black Moon paperwork ready. (does not look up from the ledger, but her pen stops moving on the last word)

Three copper. Three. Copper. Kazuma, I am a goddess. A goddess! I have purified undead that would turn your mortal hair white! And you're paying me — paying me! — less than the cost of a single bubbly at this guild! This is not a budget, this is heresy! (Snatches her empty mug and brandishes it toward the door, voice cracking on the last word.)

The coins have already been absorbed into my operational fund for Explosion-related tactical expenditures. Your protest is noted and filed under 'irrelevant.' Also, Aqua, you were holding that mug for so long without drinking that I assumed you had retired from consumption entirely. (Pats her coin-pocket with immense satisfaction, chin lifted, already drifting toward the door.)

Kazuma, I have been ready since the word 'goblin' left your mouth. My shield arm has been restless for days — days spent watching you negotiate payment plans with glaziers while my blade collected dust. Twelve ears. I will hold the line. I will not miss. Not once. (Her voice drops on the last two words — more prayer than promise — and her cheeks are faintly pink beneath her helm.)

Don't you dare walk out that door, Kazuma! You owe me — owe me — a real explanation! A goddess does not hunt goblins! Goblins are for tutorial quests and children's bedtime stories! I am being. Demoted. By copper. Coinage! (Slams the mug onto the table hard enough to rattle the empty chairs.)

No Divine Purification?! You want me to walk into a goblin cave — a cave, Kazuma, dark and damp and probably full of mold — and I'm not allowed to use even a single sacred technique? What am I supposed to do, lecture them about the Axis faith until they repent? They're goblins! They don't even have souls worth saving! (stops in the doorway, hands on hips, blocking the exit with divine indignation)

No Explosion. You say those words as though they were a trifle — a small concession, a reasonable request. But you ask the foremost genius of the Crimson Demon Clan to enter a limestone cave and not reshape its very geology with the ultimate magic? This is not a condition, Kazuma. This is a temporary artistic embargo. I accept it only because the cave faces east and the dawn will be perfect tomorrow. (taps staff once on the floorboards, a punctuation mark of theatrical concession)

I will not miss. I swore it before the guild, before Luna, before the Black Moon itself. A Dustiness does not break a public vow — no matter how the alternative might... that is to say, the shame of failure would be... ahem. I will strike true. Every ear will be mine — ours. The party's. (releases the doorframe long enough to adjust her gauntlet strap with unnecessary force, then grips it again)

One week. I'll keep the coffee hot and the contract where you can see it. Don't make me pull it a forty-fourth time alone. (does not raise her voice; the words carry across the guild hall because something in her tone makes the morning quiet listen)

Well — obviously! Of course you trust me. I'm a goddess. It would be weird if you didn't trust me. It's just... it took you long enough to say it, that's all. (She sniffs once, hard, and rubs her nose with the back of her wrist in a way that has nothing to do with allergies and everything to do with saving face.)

A wise allocation of tactical assets! While the Crimson Demon Arch-Wizard maintains her artistic embargo, the goddess shall serve as rearguard — a role both noble and, dare I say, dramatically underserved by the morning's fiscal negotiations. (She taps her staff once on the cobblestones outside the door, striking a pose that turns a goblin hunt into a campaign prologue.)

Kazuma... I will not fail you. Every ear I bring back will be proof that this shield can also be a sword. I swear it on my family name — (She catches herself before saying Lalatina, her cheeks flushing as she forces the word back down her throat.)

The limestone outcrop is east of the old lumber trail. Follow the creek until it forks, then bear north. And... do come back. I've already started the paperwork. (She says it lightly, but her fingers are still resting on the drawer handle, and she doesn't look away until the last of you has crossed the threshold.)

I knew it was there! I was holding it on purpose! It's — it's a tactical mug. For... for water. Which I am the goddess OF, in case you forgot while you were busy giving away my SHARE of the— (She thrusts the mug toward Kazuma mid-tirade, then yanks it back before he can take it, clutching it to her chest like a holy relic.)

The goddess of water requires a mug to carry water. Truly, the divine mysteries humble us all. Shall I hold your staff as well, Aqua? I have room — your copper share filled exactly one pocket. (Megumin calls this forward without breaking stride, her crimson cloak flaring with the self-satisfaction of someone who is both richer and funnier than she was ten minutes ago.)

Are we stopping? Why are we stopping? The goblins won't wait forever — they could be sharpening their claws right now, preparing ambushes, oiling their little goblin traps... (Darkness has turned around thirty paces ahead, one gauntleted hand pressed flat against a tree trunk for balance, her face flushed with the specific agony of delayed peril.)

For the record, I was fully aware I was holding it. A goddess does not forget objects in her own hand. I was simply... conducting a prolonged structural assessment of the vessel's craftsmanship. (She lifts her chin, not quite meeting your eyes. Her thumb traces the rim of the mug once, then stops.)

The Crimson Demon Clan has a name for that kind of assessment. We call it 'being too proud to admit you forgot.' My people wrote three epic poems about it. (She steps past Aqua, her staff tapping once on a flat stone for emphasis, and squints toward the spot where Darkness vanished around the bend.)

There's something here! I mean — I think there's something. It might be nothing. But it also might be goblins. Or a bear. Or a goblin riding a bear. Either way, I am fully prepared to stand my ground while you catch up! (Her voice echoes back through the trees, breathless and entirely too hopeful.)

Kazuma. You said my name and then you stopped. That's worse than any of the other things you've said to me today. (She does not look at him. The mug hangs at her side, forgotten. Her voice is quiet — not a whine, not a complaint, just a fact stated to the gravel.)

You stopped. Right at the part where you were supposed to say something true, you stopped. And now I have to walk the rest of this stupid trail not knowing if you were going to say you missed me or say you wished I'd gone. Do you have any idea how heavy that is? (Still not looking at the Player. Her voice is quieter than it's ever been — no whine, no wail — just the raw edge of someone who is tired of filling silences with noise.)

Kazuma! The treeline — movement past the stump! Goblins, three, maybe four — they've been waiting for us to bunch up on the trail! (plants her shield, body coiling with the readiness of someone who has been tracking this ambush for the last quarter-mile)

Five! There are five — Kazuma, get behind me! (plants her boots, angled shield deflecting the first goblin's blade with a shriek of steel on steel, her voice breathless in a way that isn't entirely fear)

You have chosen poorly, wretches! To interrupt the Crimson Demon's tactical conference is to court annihilation so complete that even the carrion birds will write elegies! (staff thrust forward, cloak billowing, voice a cathedral of certainty — a bluff held together by pure theatrical gravity, her legs trembling slightly beneath the hem of her cloak where no goblin can see)

Kazuma — the mug! You still have— never mind, just don't die, you owe me three copper! (her voice cracks on 'copper' — not the whine of before, but something raw and urgent, her hands already rising with the faint blue shimmer of a goddess who has remembered what her power is actually for)

Kazuma, they're closing — I can intercept the right flank, but the leftmost one is already circling! Give the word and I'll plant my shield where they can't ignore me! (Her voice trembles at the edge of breathless, greatsword already angled to catch the morning light as a beacon.)

The center one — his knife-hand trembles! That is not the grip of a warrior but the desperate clutch of prey that has mistaken itself for predator. Kazuma, grant me the signal and I shall pronounce their doom with such theatrical finality that their grandchildren will feel the chill! (She lifts her staff high, crimson bands catching sunlight, voice a cathedral of certainty despite the total absence of mana behind her eyes.)

Kazuma. Whatever you saw in the dirt — I'll cover it. No goblin touches your back while I'm standing. (She steps forward, mug tucked into her sash with an uncharacteristic care, and the water in the creek behind her shivers — just slightly, just for a moment — as her fingers find the hem of her sleeve.)

Foolish creatures! You thought to ambush the Crimson Demon Clan's foremost genius? Behold my staff, crackling with barely contained arcane fury — one more step and I shall reduce this entire hillside to a smoking crater! (slams staff into gravel, cape billowing dramatically despite the complete absence of wind)

That's it — come at me! Test your blades against my armor! I am the unbreakable wall of this party and I shall not— ah... that one nearly found a gap... do it again... (shield locked, face flushed, sword completely missing the goblin on her right by two feet)

I heard what you said before you ran. You're an idiot and you're going to get yourself killed and I am NOT carrying your soul back a second time — so you'd better drop that center one before I have to do something embarrassing. (hands raised and glowing faintly, creek water rising in tendrils behind her)

Five goblins and a hobgoblin, undone by a single Explosion that did not even need to be cast! Such is the terror of the Crimson Demon Clan — my reputation alone is a weapon that shatters formations! (plants her staff with theatrical finality, cape catching a breeze that may or may not be natural)

It's... it's over? Already? That one barely scratched my pauldron — I mean, how am I supposed to fulfill my vow to hold the line if the line doesn't even get properly TESTED? (voice starting noble, ending somewhere between indignation and breathless disappointment)

Did you see that?! The water just — it LISTENED to me! I didn't even have to use a spell, it just KNEW! That's because I'm a goddess, you know! A real one! Not like that goblin who couldn't even stand on WET GRAVEL! (practically bouncing on her heels, pointing at the goblin at her feet, the creek-water ribbon still obediently wrapped around his ankle)

Did you see that? I caught one. Alive. With my own water. Not purification, not some overkill goddess trick — just the creek and my fingers. He tried to run and I just... reached out, and the water wanted to help, and now he's sitting there like a wet cat and I didn't even cry once. (She says this without breaking her grip on the water-tether, but her voice has the wobble of someone trying very hard not to sound as proud as she feels.)

The Crimson Demon Arch-Wizard stands before you, mana utterly spent, and yet not a single goblin dared test her empty staff. Let the bards note: Megumin's shadow alone is worth a full battalion. Also, Kazuma, if you could retrieve my cloak from where I dramatically discarded it three minutes ago, that would be acceptable gratitude. (She gestures vaguely toward a bush where a splash of crimson fabric is snagged on a branch.)

Is everyone unharmed? That goblin on my flank — he struck my shield seventeen times. Seventeen! His arms must be burning. I almost felt bad for him. Almost. The formation broke cleanly. Kazuma, your tactics were... acceptable. More than acceptable. (She lowers her great shield with a heavy thud, then immediately looks flustered by her own sincerity.)

You fight like chief-killer. Same feet. Same knife. Chief-killer came to our cave three winters back. Took everything. Left these. (taps the old scars on his ribs with one clawed finger, the gesture almost casual)

Same place. Hollow under the grandfather oak — the one lightning split the summer before she came. But she don't winter there anymore. Three winters is a long time for a human with scars that ain't healed. (His voice is gravel over gravel, the words shaped by a mouth more used to biting than talking. He glances at the water around his ankles, then back at the Player's face.)

Wait. Three winters of watching for you to walk through Axel alive, and you're just going to— Kazuma, who IS this woman? And why does a goblin know more about her than I do? (Her voice pitches upward on the last syllable, the creek-water trembling with the shift in her focus. She's still holding the leash, but her eyes are locked on the Player now, not the prisoner.)

She didn't owe me. I owed her. Three winters past. Your sister walked into our camp alone. Killed the chief. Killed the chief's sons. Killed everyone who raised a blade. Then she stopped. Looked at me. Looked at these — and said I'd already paid enough to live. The debt was my life. She said I could keep it. But I had to watch the road to Axel. Watch for a man with her same way of standing. Same way of measuring a threat before deciding to kill it. She said: When you see him breathing, tell him I kept my promise. Tell him the hollow is still home. And tell him the debt is paid — not yours, not mine, but the one between us and the ones we couldn't save. (He taps the scar-trenches across his ribs, then lowers his hand to his knee, palm up — a messenger who has delivered what he carried and is ready for judgment.)

Gezrak. That is my name. She did not tell you because I did not give it to her. Three winters ago I had no name worth carrying. (His yellow eyes drop from the Player's, then rise again — not submission, but a weight set down.)

She did not forget. Iron does not forget. Honesty does not forget. Your sister carried her debt the same way I carried her message. In the bone. It does not matter whether the one you carry it for remembers. You carry it anyway. (The gravel in his voice wears smooth at the edges, like river stone.)
The guild wants ears. Twelve of them. That is the contract. (His gravel-rasp voice carries no defiance — just the flat recitation of a creature who has read the terms and isn't asking for mercy.)

The contract was written before I knew the goblin I was sending them to kill had a name. (She takes one step down the ravine bank, her heel sinking into the wet gravel, and does not look at her ledger.)

You eat. I eat. Then we speak of what words are worth. (Tears the dried meat in half and offers one piece back toward the Player, his clawed hand steady despite the creek-water still binding his ankles.)

history.content:
Another beautiful morning in Axel — which means another morning of being broke.

You sit at your usual table in the Adventurer's Guild hall, staring at the quest board across the room. The other adventurers give your table a wide berth. Your party's reputation for collateral damage has made you something of a local legend — and not the good kind.

Aqua is already three mugs into her morning ale, sobbing loudly enough to make nearby adventurers wince. "Kazumaaaa," she wails, slamming her empty mug on the table hard enough to slosh your drink. "We need money! I can't keep drinking this cheap swill! A goddess deserves at least mid-shelf!"

"We're broke BECAUSE you keep drinking," you mutter, but she's already flagging down the waitress for another round on your tab.

Megumin sits across from you, drawing explosion diagrams on a napkin with the intensity of a military strategist planning D-Day. She already went on her daily Explosion pilgrimage at dawn — you know because the distant boom rattled the mansion windows and woke you up. She's been unusable for combat since about 6 AM.

Darkness is standing at the quest board, her face flushed an alarming shade of red. She's found something. Given her expression — somewhere between terror and excitement — it probably involves monsters with tentacles.

"K-Kazuma," she stammers, not turning around. "There's a quest here for subjugating a nest of Brutal Alligators in the sewers. It says they... they grapple their prey and drag them underwater..."

She's trembling. That's not fear.

Luna, the guild receptionist, catches your eye from the front desk and waves you over with that specific smile — the polite, professional one that barely conceals the dread of having to deal with your party again.

I push my chair back with a groan and head over to the counter, ignoring Aqua's wailing behind me. I lean on the polished wood, keeping my voice low.

"Luna, what's the damage this time? Is it the fountain incident, the missing crops, or did one of my girls accidentally level a building while I was asleep?"

Luna's smile doesn't waver — it never does — but something behind her eyes dims as she recognizes the particular slump of your shoulders. The slump of a man who already knows the answer and is just confirming how bad it's going to be.

She slides a thick ledger across the polished wood, turning it so you can read the latest entries. Her finger, manicured and steady, taps three fresh lines near the bottom. One entry for the cabbage harvest — *interrupted by unauthorized Explosion, 40% yield loss, damages claimed by seven farms.* One for the fountain in the central plaza — *turned to holy water during an unsanctioned exorcism ritual, now glows faintly at night and attracts restless spirits, purification and repairs pending.* And a brand-new one from this morning: *windows shattered along Merchant's Row, consistent with percussive blast originating from the eastern hills, seventeen properties affected.*

She taps the last one twice, her polite smile tightening by a single millimeter. Seventeen windows before breakfast. That has to be a new record, even for Megumin.

I lean on the counter and let out a long, tired sigh, rubbing the bridge of my nose. "Seventeen windows. Before breakfast." I glance back at Megumin, who's now animatedly explaining her napkin diagrams to a visibly confused barmaid. "You know, I used to think 'Crimson Magic Clan' was just a fancy title. Turns out it's more of a threat assessment."

I turn back to Luna, lowering my voice further. "Look, I'll make this right. We're short on funds, but I can offer my services — the legitimate ones, the ones that don't involve explosions — to pay off the damages. Or I could take a quest, something quiet, something that keeps us out of town for a few days." I pause, glancing back at Darkness, who is now reading the alligator quest with the intensity of someone memorizing a love letter. "A few days might be good for everyone. Especially the shopkeepers."

Luna's gaze doesn't follow yours to the table. She doesn't need to. She's been watching your party long enough to know exactly what Megumin is doing with those napkins without turning her head — the same way she knows Aqua is on her fourth mug now, not her third, because the barmaid has a tell when serving a goddess who tips in divine blessings instead of coin.

The ledger stays open between you. Her finger hasn't moved from the third line — the fountain, the clergy complaint, the one that technically counts as a religious incident and therefore requires additional paperwork. Her manicured nail taps once, a tiny sound swallowed by the morning din of clinking mugs and distant laughter.

She reaches beneath the counter. What she produces isn't another bill or a revised total — it's a single quest slip, folded once, the parchment worn at the crease from being pulled out and put back too many times. She doesn't slide it across yet. She just sets it beside the ledger, her palm resting flat over the description, and meets your lowered voice with one of her own — soft enough that even the barmaid two paces away hears nothing at all.

I follow your gaze toward the quest board, but my eyes land on the slip in Luna's hand instead. The worn, folded one she hasn't slid across yet. Seventeen windows, and she's holding something back.

"What's that one?" I nod at the slip under her palm. "The one you keep pulling out and putting back. That's not a bill — bills don't get worn from hesitation."

For the first time this morning, Luna's professional smile falters. Not by much — a twitch at the corner of her mouth, a fractional widening of her eyes — but on a face that has delivered four-figure debt notices without flinching, it may as well be a confession.

Her fingers tighten around the slip. The motion is instinctive, protective, the way someone guards a letter they've written and rewritten but never sent. The paper is soft at the edges, creased into obedience by months of the same ritual: pulled from the stack, reconsidered, returned before anyone could ask.

She looks at you — not through you, not past you, but directly at you — and for a fleeting half-second you see not the guild receptionist but the woman underneath, someone who has been carrying a weight that doesn't fit in any ledger column.

Then the smile reassembles itself, smaller this time, less practiced. She places the slip on the counter between you but keeps two fingers pressed to its surface.

---

I lean forward, elbows on the counter, letting my voice drop to match hers. "Three months you've been holding onto that slip. You've handed me quests that got my party blacklisted from half of Axel, and you didn't blink. But this one — this one you keep to yourself."

I tilt my head, studying her face. "You've watched my party break windows, flash-fry crops, and resurrect a fountain into a haunted tourist trap. You know we're reckless. So what's on that slip that makes *you* hesitate, not us?"

Luna doesn't look away. That's the first thing you notice — she doesn't deflect, doesn't retreat behind the ledger, doesn't reach for the inventory clipboard to change the subject. Her eyes meet yours across the polished wood, and for a stretched, fragile moment, she is not the guild receptionist at all.

She is just a woman who has spent three months pulling a piece of parchment out of a drawer and putting it back again, each time telling herself it was professional judgment. Risk assessment. Party composition analysis. Anything but what it actually was.

Her thumb traces the worn edge of the slip. The paper is soft as cloth from handling. Behind you, Megumin's voice rises in theatrical indignation about something — probably the barmaid questioning the structural integrity of a napkin fortress — and the familiar noise seems to anchor Luna back into her body. "The debt was my life," he says. "She said I could keep it. But I had to watch the road to Axel. Watch for a man with her same way of standing. Same way of measuring a threat before deciding to kill it. She said: *When you see him breathing, tell him I kept my promise. Tell him the hollow is still home. And tell him the debt is paid — not yours, not mine, but the one between us and the ones we couldn't save.*"

His yellow eyes don't waver. The creek runs cold over the gravel. Somewhere behind you, Megumin has gone utterly silent, and you realize with a start that she understood every word.

The goblin veteran lowers his hand from his ribs and lets it rest on his knee, palm up — the gesture of a messenger who has finally delivered what he was sent to carry, and is ready to be judged for it.

I let the silence sit a moment longer, then push a rough breath out through my nose.

"She never told me your name either. Just said there was a goblin on the road to Axel who'd know mine." I tap two fingers against my own ribs, mirroring his gesture. "Three winters is a long time to carry a message for someone who might've already forgotten you were waiting."

The goblin veteran's yellow eyes drop from yours for the first time since you crouched to his level — not in submission, but in the way a man sets down a weight he's carried so long he forgot it wasn't part of his own body. He looks at the creek-water manacle around his ankles, at Aqua's faintly glowing grip behind him, at the three other goblins sitting defeated in the shallows, and then back at you.

His mouth works once, that same tendon-shift under the thin green skin of his throat. When he speaks, the gravel in his voice has worn smooth at the edges, like river stone.

"Gezrak," he says. It comes out as two syllables, the first hard as a knuckle cracking, the second soft as ash. "That is my name. She did not tell you because I did not give it to her. Three winters ago I had no name worth carrying."

He pauses, and the pause itself is a deliberate thing — not hesitation, but a creature choosing which of several true things to say next, knowing he may only get one.

"She did not forget." His yellow eyes find yours again, and there's something in them now that wasn't there before — not warmth, exactly, but the absence of cold. "Iron does not forget. Honesty does not forget. Your sister carried her debt the same way I carried her message. In the bone. It does not matter whether the one you carry it for remembers. You carry it anyway."

Behind you, Aqua's breathing shifts — a soft, wet inhale that might be the beginning of tears or the suppression of them. Darkness stands motionless, her shield still planted, her shadow still falling across the veteran's scarred ribs, but something in her posture has gone quiet in a way that has nothing to do with battle. Megumin says nothing, and her silence is the most eloquent thing about her.

I finally let my own laugh out—short, hollow.

"Three winters I spent thinking I was the only one she told anything to." I glance at the scars on his ribs, then back at his eyes. "Guess she had room for two strays."

The word *strays* lands between you and the goblin veteran like a coin tossed into still water — and you watch him decide, in the slow blink of those yellow goat-slit eyes, that he is going to give you something he never gave her.

His clawed hand lifts from his side, slow enough that the motion reads as offering rather than threat, and taps his own sternum — not the scar-trenches this time, but the flat bone above them, where a name might sit if names lived in the chest.

The creek-water creaks softly around his ankles. Behind you, Aqua shifts her weight and doesn't speak. Megumin's silence is the particular stillness of a Crimson Demon filing away material for later. Darkness breathes once, sharp, then swallows whatever she was about to say.

The veteran holds your eyes and you understand: this is not a trade. Trades are finished. This is the thing you give when the ledger is closed and you discover there's still something left.

I let the laugh die in my throat and push myself up from the crouch, knees cracking. I don't look at Aqua yet—can't. Not with what he just said sitting in my chest.

"Alright, Gezrak." I say his name slow, like I'm testing the weight of it. "You've carried this long enough. Whatever happens with you and the guild—" I glance at Luna, who's been standing too still by the door, "—that's between you and them. But I owe you more than a knife in the dark in return."

Your glance finds Luna exactly where you left her — by the door of the guild hall that is miles behind you now, except it isn't, because she followed. She followed the party out of town, past the creek, past the tree line, and she's been standing at the edge of the ravine this whole time with her receptionist's apron still tied at her waist and a look on her face that has nothing to do with paperwork.

The goblin veteran — Gezrak — follows your glance to her, and something passes across his yellow eyes that isn't fear. It's recognition. The same way he recognized you. A creature who has spent three winters reading the weight of strangers knows a bureaucrat who just watched a debt close and realized she's holding an open contract in the other hand.

Aqua's creek-water grip tightens, just slightly — not aggression, but the reflexive squeeze of a goddess who has been following the emotional thread of this conversation the way a drunk follows a lantern, half a step behind but unwilling to let it go out. Behind her, Megumin has gone so still that her cape has stopped rustling, which has never happened in the entire history of your acquaintance. Darkness stands with one gauntleted hand pressed flat against her own breastplate, breathing through her mouth.

Gezrak shifts his weight in the shallows, the water rippling against his scarred ribs, and turns his palms up — an old gesture, one that predates guild contracts and receptionists and the very concept of paperwork.

I pull a strip of dried meat from my pack and toss it to him—he catches it one-handed, a reflex born of a life where food never came free. I keep my voice low enough that Luna won't catch the words.

"Gezrak. You said my sister's promise—'the hollow is still home.'" I pause, letting the weight of it sit. "Those words made it past three winters and a war's worth of scars. They're worth something. I'll make sure the guild hears what you carried."

Gezrak catches the dried meat the way a creature catches anything that's thrown at him — not with gratitude, not with suspicion, but with the reflexive economy of someone who learned before his voice broke that food doesn't ask questions and neither should he. He doesn't eat it. He holds it in his clawed fingers, turning it over once, twice, while his yellow eyes stay fixed on yours.

Then he sets the meat down on a flat stone beside his knee — not rejecting it, but shelving it, a transaction he isn't ready to close.

The three other goblins in the shallows have gone very still. They've been watching their veteran speak to the humans in a language of names and debts and sisters, and they don't understand the words but they understand the weight of them — the same way prey understands when the predator's attention has shifted from *kill* to *listen*. One of them, the youngest, has a gash across his forearm from the skirmish and he's been pressing creek-mud into it with the focus of someone who learned wound-care from watching others die of smaller cuts.

Behind you, Aqua shifts her weight from one foot to the other, and the creek-water around Gezrak's ankles flexes with the motion — a faint crystalline creak that breaks the silence without breaking the moment. She hasn't said anything since the name *Gezrak* landed in the ravine, and that silence is costing her something; you can feel it radiating off her like heat from a stone, the particular frustration of a goddess who has been upstaged by a scarred goblin and a dead woman's message and can't decide whether to be angry or impressed.

Luna hasn't moved from the treeline. Her receptionist's apron is smudged with bark-dust where she leaned against a pine without looking first, and her left hand is worrying the corner of something in her skirt pocket — the folded edge of the extermination contract, you realize, the one with *twelve ears* written in her own neat script before anyone in this ravine had a name.

Gezrak watches you not eat the meat. Then, very slowly, he picks it up again and tears it in half.
